questions.text: Do you believe intelligence is something you're born with or something you can develop?

options.text: You're either smart or you're not — can't really change it
Some people are naturally smarter, but you can improve a little
Intelligence can grow with effort, but there are limits
Anyone can become significantly smarter with the right methods
Intelligence is 100% buildable — your brain literally grows with practice

questions.text: When you see a topper, what's your first thought?

options.text: They're just naturally gifted — I could never be like them
They probably have better resources or tuition than me
They work hard, but they also have some natural advantage
They've figured out better strategies — I can learn those too
They simply put in more deliberate effort — I can do the same if I commit

questions.text: How do you feel when a subject is very difficult for you?

options.text: This subject isn't for me — I'm just not built for it
I'll try, but I don't expect to do well
It's hard but I'll manage somehow
Difficulty means I need to change my approach, not give up
The harder it is, the more my brain is growing — I welcome the struggle

questions.text: When you score poorly on a test, you think:

options.text: I'm stupid — this proves I'm not good enough
Bad luck — the paper was too hard this time
I'll try to do better next time
Let me analyze exactly which concepts I got wrong and fix them
This is valuable data — now I know my weak spots and can target them precisely

questions.text: After failing at something, how long does it take you to try again?

options.text: I usually give up and avoid that thing
Weeks or months — I need time to recover emotionally
A few days — once I stop feeling bad about it
Within a day — I adjust my approach and try differently
Immediately — failure is just feedback, I iterate right away

questions.text: Do you believe luck plays a big role in academic success?

options.text: Yes — lucky people get easy papers, good teachers, and opportunities
Luck matters a lot but effort matters too
It's roughly 50-50 luck and effort
Effort matters much more — you create your own luck through preparation
Luck is what happens when preparation meets opportunity — I focus only on preparation

questions.text: How do you feel about putting in effort when results aren't immediate?

options.text: If I don't see results quickly, I lose motivation and stop
I get frustrated and start questioning if it's worth it
I can keep going for a while but eventually lose steam
I trust the process — results are delayed but certain if I persist
I focus on daily systems, not outcomes — the score takes care of itself

questions.text: On a day when you feel zero motivation, you:

options.text: Skip studying — you can't study without motivation
Scroll your phone and promise to start tomorrow
Try but usually give up after 10-15 minutes
Use discipline — motivation is unreliable, habits are not
Show up anyway and do even a reduced session — consistency beats intensity

questions.text: What does 'hard work' mean to you?

options.text: Sitting with books for long hours (even if distracted)
Reading everything multiple times
Spending more time on subjects I find difficult
Working with focus, using proven strategies, and measuring progress
Deliberate practice on weaknesses + smart strategy + consistent daily execution

questions.text: What's your goal when you study?

options.text: Just pass the exam somehow
Get decent marks — not fail, not top
Score above average
Score in the top 10% — I set high standards for myself
Master the subject deeply — marks are a byproduct of real understanding

questions.text: When you achieve a goal, you:

options.text: Relax and take it easy for a long time
Feel satisfied and coast for a while
Celebrate briefly then continue as normal
Celebrate, then immediately set a higher goal
Appreciate the win but know there's always the next level — I never fully 'arrive'

questions.text: How do you compare yourself to others?

options.text: I compare and feel bad — others are always better
I try not to compare but end up doing it negatively
I compare sometimes but it doesn't affect me much
I compare only to learn — what are they doing differently that I can adopt?
My only competition is yesterday's version of myself

questions.text: When studying a topic, how deep do you go?

options.text: Just enough to recognize the answer in MCQs
I memorize the key points and definitions
I understand the concept reasonably well
I understand it deeply enough to explain it to someone else
I understand it so well I could apply it to problems I've never seen before

questions.text: Do you seek feedback on your work?

options.text: No — I avoid feedback because it feels like criticism
Only when it's required (teacher corrections)
Sometimes — from friends or when I'm unsure
Regularly — I actively ask teachers and peers to point out my mistakes
I chase feedback aggressively — every mistake found is a gift that prevents future failure

questions.text: How do you feel about asking for help?

options.text: It's embarrassing — it means I'm dumb
I avoid it unless absolutely necessary
I ask sometimes but feel uncomfortable
I ask freely — getting help is smart, not weak
I proactively seek mentors, peer groups, and resources — leverage is intelligence

questions.text: When your results are poor, who is responsible?

options.text: The teacher — they didn't teach well
The system — the exam was unfair
Partly me, partly circumstances
Mostly me — I could have prepared better regardless of circumstances
100% me — I own my results completely. External factors exist but I choose my response

questions.text: Do you believe you control your academic destiny?

options.text: No — too many things are out of my control
Partially — but the system is stacked against people like me
Somewhat — I can influence it but not fully control it
Mostly yes — my daily choices determine my outcomes
Absolutely — I am the architect of my results. Period.

questions.text: When things go wrong (bad health, family issues, distractions), you:

options.text: Use it as a reason to give up or lower expectations
Feel helpless and wait for things to get better
Adjust my expectations and do what I can
Acknowledge the challenge but find a way to keep moving forward
Adapt immediately — obstacles are part of the game, not exceptions to it

questions.text: How far ahead do you plan your academic journey?

options.text: I don't plan — I deal with whatever comes
A few days or weeks before exams
One semester at a time
1-2 years ahead with clear milestones
I have a 5+ year vision and reverse-engineer my daily actions from it

questions.text: What drives you to study?

options.text: Parental pressure or fear of punishment
Not wanting to fail or be embarrassed
Getting a decent job and stable life
Achieving something meaningful and proving what I'm capable of
A deep personal mission — I want to master my field and make an impact

bands.label: 🏆 Topper Mindset
bands.text: You think like a topper. You believe in growth, own your results, embrace failure as feedback, and set audacious standards. Keep this mindset and combine it with smart strategy — results will follow inevitably.

bands.label: 📈 Growth Mindset (Almost There)
bands.text: You're close to a topper mindset but some limiting beliefs are still holding you back. Look at the domains marked orange/red below — fixing even ONE of those areas could dramatically shift your trajectory.

bands.label: 😐 Average/Comfort Zone Mindset
bands.text: You're stuck in an average comfort zone. Not because you lack ability, but because your beliefs, standards, and responses keep you playing safe. The difference between you and a topper isn't talent — it's these exact mindset patterns. The good news: they're all changeable.

bands.label: ⚠️ Fixed/Mediocre Mindset
bands.text: Your current mindset is keeping you trapped in mediocrity. You believe ability is fixed, avoid failure, rely on motivation, and blame circumstances. None of these are character flaws — they're LEARNED patterns that can be UNLEARNED. Start with one domain below and commit to changing it for 30 days.

Beliefs About Ability.mediocre: You believe talent is fixed. This single belief limits everything else — if you think you can't grow, you won't try hard enough. The truth: your brain physically changes with practice.
Beliefs About Ability.average: You partially believe in growth but still doubt your potential. Start tracking your progress weekly to build evidence that YOU can improve.
Beliefs About Ability.topper: You fully embrace the growth mindset. You know ability is built, not born. This belief alone gives you an unfair advantage.
Beliefs About Ability.fix: Read about neuroplasticity. Your brain literally grows new connections every time you practice. Intelligence is a muscle, not a gift.

Response to Failure.mediocre: You see failure as proof you're not good enough. This makes you avoid challenges and give up early. Toppers see failure as data — nothing more.
Response to Failure.average: You recover from failure but slowly. Shortening your recovery time from days to hours is what separates good from great.
Response to Failure.topper: You treat failure as fuel. Every setback gives you precise information about what to fix. You iterate rapidly.
Response to Failure.fix: After every setback, write: 'What specifically went wrong? What will I do differently?' Then act within 24 hours.

Effort & Discipline.mediocre: You rely on motivation and do long unfocused hours. Toppers rely on systems and do short, intense, deliberate sessions every single day.
Effort & Discipline.average: You put in effort but inconsistently. The gap between you and a topper isn't talent — it's showing up on the days you don't feel like it.
Effort & Discipline.topper: You've built discipline as a habit. You don't wait to 'feel like it' — you execute regardless. This is your superpower.
Effort & Discipline.fix: Build a non-negotiable daily minimum (even 45 min). Track your streak. Never break the chain — consistency compounds.

Goals & Standards.mediocre: Your standards are low — 'just pass' or 'above average'. You'll always perform to the level of your expectations. Raise the bar.
Goals & Standards.average: You aim reasonably high but don't push beyond comfort. Toppers set standards that make them uncomfortable — that's where growth lives.
Goals & Standards.topper: You set audacious goals and hold yourself to high standards. You compete with your potential, not your peers.
Goals & Standards.fix: Write your goal as: 'Top 5% in [subject]'. Then ask: What would someone at that level do daily? Do that.

Learning Approach.mediocre: You study to recognize answers, not to understand deeply. This creates fragile knowledge that collapses under exam pressure.
Learning Approach.average: You understand concepts but don't push to mastery. Toppers study until they can teach it, apply it to unseen problems, and explain WHY it works.
Learning Approach.topper: You pursue deep understanding and actively seek feedback. Your learning is active, strategic, and efficient.
Learning Approach.fix: For every topic, pass the 'teach test': Can you explain it simply to a 10-year-old? If not, you don't truly understand it yet.

Ownership & Responsibility.mediocre: You blame external factors for poor results. As long as you do this, you give away your power to change. Take it back.
Ownership & Responsibility.average: You take partial responsibility but still make excuses sometimes. Full ownership is the bridge between average and excellent.
Ownership & Responsibility.topper: You own your results completely. You don't waste energy on blame — you invest it in solutions. This is true maturity.
Ownership & Responsibility.fix: Repeat: 'I am 100% responsible for my results. Circumstances explain, they never excuse.' Act from this belief daily.

Long-term Vision.mediocre: You have no clear direction — just reacting to deadlines and pressure. Without a vision, every day feels pointless. Create one.
Long-term Vision.average: You have some goals but they're vague or short-term. A clear long-term vision turns daily tasks from chores into stepping stones.
Long-term Vision.topper: You have a compelling long-term vision and reverse-engineer your daily actions from it. Every hour of study connects to a larger purpose.
Long-term Vision.fix: Write: 'In 5 years, I want to ___.' Then: 'In 1 year, I need to ___.' Then: 'This month, I must ___.' Then: 'Today, I will ___.'
